Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Name at the start that this is personal for some people and anyone can step out. Keep every example about the characters. If a student discloses something, don’t promise secrecy; walk them to a counselor that day.

Every student in the room

What stepping in looks like depends on who you are: speaking up to an older student, or with police nearby, costs some students more than others, so treat distract and delegate as full answers, not the backup plan.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can say what respect looks like in action, for themselves and for other people; explain why people freeze when others are watching, and why someone usually does step in; pick one of three ways to step in (direct, distract, delegate) that fits them; and hold or respect a "not ready" without guilt.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 3 minBefore we start
  2. 5 minA time you felt respected: turn and talk, share out
  3. 3 minRespect goes both ways
  4. 5 minThe smoke room, and the real result
  5. 6 minWhich reason gets you most? Turn and talk, share out
  6. 4 minSomeone usually steps in, and three ways in
  7. 14 minFour moments: the screenshot, upstairs, “come on,” lucky
  8. 5 minEvery student, where else this shows up, close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Before we start, the smoke room, someone usually steps in, three ways in, two of the four moments, and the close.

Before you teach
Assume someone in the room has lived this.

A screenshot passed around, a night at a party, a partner who sulked until they got a yes. Say at the start that nobody will be asked about their own life, anyone can step out, and every example stays with the characters.

Say "not your fault" out loud.

When you get to Ellie, Maya, Riley and Ethan, say it plainly: what someone drank, sent or said earlier never makes it their fault. Someone in the room may need to hear it from an adult.

Bystanders who froze are in the room too.

Some students have watched something and done nothing, and still carry it. Name it once: "Almost everyone has frozen. A late check-in still counts." Then keep moving.

If a student tells you something.

Thank them, stay calm, and don't promise to keep it secret. Walk them to a counselor that day. Counselors can explain up front what they'd have to share and with whom.

Keep "Just Talk" about the behavior.

If a student defends ranking as a joke, answer with what it does to the person who overhears it, not with a judgment about the student. Then move on.

Use anonymous cards for the hard questions.

Ninth graders will ask more on a card than out loud. Read cards before answering, and skip any that name a real person.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Stepping in isn't the same for everyone.

In some families, correcting an older student or an adult in public is disrespectful. Some students fear what calling police could mean for them or their family. Distract and delegate count as much as direct. Say so.

Every gender.

Boys and nonbinary students are pressured, photographed and assaulted too, and are less likely to tell. Ethan's story is there on purpose. Riley's gender isn't named; leave it that way.

LGBTQ+ students.

Outing someone, or threatening to, is a form of pressure and a respect violation. If you add examples, include same-gender couples.

Faith and family values.

Some students come from families or faiths where dating isn't allowed yet. Respect, saying no and not sharing photos apply to everyone, dating or not. Never assume students are sexually active.

Disability and neurodivergence.

Students who read social cues differently may miss when a joke has turned cruel, or may be the target of one. Concrete lines to say help everyone. A disability doesn't take away anyone's right to say yes or no.

Who they tell first.

Depending on family and culture, a student might tell a friend, sibling, cousin, coach, faith leader or counselor first. Any first person counts.

What the research says

When smoke poured into a room, 75% of students sitting alone reported it. With two people who calmly ignored it, 10% did.

Latané and Darley, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1968

When students thought they were the only one who heard someone having a seizure, 85% went for help. When they thought four others heard it too, 31% did.

Darley and Latané, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1968

A review of more than 7,700 people found the bystander effect is weaker when the danger is obvious, and weaker among people who know each other.

Fischer et al., Psychological Bulletin, 2011

In security footage of 219 real public fights in three countries, at least one bystander helped in 9 of 10, and more bystanders made it more likely someone would.

Philpot et al., American Psychologist, 2020

Across 26 Kentucky high schools, schools that trained students to step in had less sexual violence in the years that followed.

Coker et al., American Journal of Preventive Medicine, 2017

Across 39 studies of more than 110,000 teens, about 12% had forwarded a sext without permission, and 8% had their own forwarded.

Madigan et al., JAMA Pediatrics, 2018
